text.p: Bergen Brunswig Corp's surprise cancellation of its $1.6 billion merger with IVAX Corp may force IVAX's new president to sell assets and take other restructuring measures, analysts said.

While the break, and Bergen's related lawsuit, may be near-term negatives for IVAX, the arrival two weeks ago of Robert Strauss as president and chief operating officer bodes well for IVAX, a Miami-based generic drug company, they said.
Strauss was chairman and chief executive of Cordis Corp, sold to Johnson & Johnson last year in a $1.9 billion stock swap, which was viewed on Wall Street as a rich deal for Cordis stockholders.

Bergen and IVAX are secretive about the reasons for the deal's breakdown. Bergen would not discuss what it described as "breaches" in the agreement and IVAX said it did not yet know what Bergen views as problems with the merger.
"From the standpoint of contrarians or bottom fishers, IVAX has a lot (of positives)." Gruntal & Co analyst David Saks said.
"The company is getting its fair share of NDA (new drug application) approvals, so the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and IVAX are in good compliance, which is very valuable."
"Over time, with better management and internal controls, it will likely turn around, but I don't know when the inflection point will be," said Saks, who rates the stock a neutral.
He cited as positives IVAX's recent FDA approval of generic versions of Zovirax, an antiviral agent, Lodine, an anti-arthritic drug and Seldane, an anithistimine.

IVAX finished unusually active American Stock Exchange trade Friday with a 1-5/8 loss at 10-3/4, while Bergen, a distributor of pharmaceuticals and other healthcare products based in Orange, Calif., ended New York Stock Exchange trade up 1/8 to 31-5/8.

The Bergen-IVAX deal was announced in November, simultaneous to IVAX's 1996 third quarter earnings, results that included a net loss of $1.47 per share after $118 million in restructuring and write-down charges. Three months earlier, IVAX said it was in technical default of its revolving credit facility, forcing the company to seek a waiver.
IVAX blamed the setbacks partly on customer inventory build-up related to the introduction in 1996 and 1995 of an unusually large number of U.S. generic drugs.

For all of 1996, IVAX lost $1.22 per share on $1.15 billion in revenues versus a 1995 profit of $0.96 per share on $1.26 billion in revenues. But IVAX significantly exceeded Wall Street earnings estimates for the 1996 fourth quarter, posting a loss of $0.02 per share versus the Zack's Investment Services consensus view of a $0.22 per share loss.

Said Hemant Shah, pharmaceutical analyst at HKS & Co: "If you read between the lines of IVAX's press release (on the Bergen deal), it says it and its advisors implemented certain strategies in anticipation of the deal potentially not going through. That could be a reason for Bergen perceiving there was a breach in the agreement.

"IVAX now has to restructure. They will have to divest assets. The company is a collection of many assets, like a chemical business, a diagnostics business, while the European assets are very valuable," Shah added.
One trader said the deal was broken and IVAX was on its own.

"I think they are going to split up the company, but whether or not it is a buy at 11 (dollars per share) is tough to say, though the company is a lot healthier than it was when it entered the agreement with Bergen."
Bergen called off the IVAX merger last night and said it will sue the Miami-based generic drug company for breaching the agreement.
A Bergen spokeswoman declined to comment further on the deal's demise or the lawsuit, which will be sealed when filed in U.S. District Court, Southern District of New York.

"We received a letter yesterday notifying us that they were unilaterally terminating the merger agreement," an IVAX spokesman said. "We have not yet been served with the lawsuit, so we do not know what their complaint is."
He declined to comment on speculation about asset sales.
((--Wall Street Desk, 212-859-1734)).
